title: Enslaved, She Sued Her Master. And Won.

beats.text: Enslaved, she sued her master. And won.

overlays.hook: Enslaved, she sued her master. *And won.*

beats.text: Meet Elizabeth Freeman. They called her Mum Bett.
For nearly thirty years, she was enslaved by Colonel John Ashley, in Sheffield, Massachusetts.
One day, Mrs. Ashley swung a red-hot shovel at a young enslaved girl. Bett took the blow, and kept the scar.
In 1780, Massachusetts adopted a new constitution. Bett heard its words: all men are born free and equal.
So she went to a lawyer, Theodore Sedgwick, and asked him to take her case.
On August 22, 1781, a jury ruled that she was not anyone's property. She was free.
Her case, and others after it, helped end slavery in Massachusetts.
She chose a new name: Elizabeth Freeman.

visual.caption: Elizabeth Freeman, by Susan Sedgwick, c. 1812

beats.text: She became a paid worker, a respected midwife, and bought her own house.
She died in 1829, and was buried in the Sedgwick family plot, the only one there not of the family.
Enslaved, she sued her master. And won.

facts.claim: Enslaved in Col. John Ashley's household, Sheffield, Massachusetts, from the 1740s; gravestone: 'remained a slave for nearly thirty years'.
Mrs. Ashley raised a red-hot kitchen shovel at another enslaved girl; Bett took the blow and bore the scar for life.
1780 Massachusetts Constitution: 'All men are born free and equal'; Bett heard it discussed.
Lawyer Theodore Sedgwick of Stockbridge took the case (with Tapping Reeve).
Brom and Bett v. Ashley; jury verdict 22 Aug 1781, Great Barrington; declared free, 30 shillings damages.
With the Quock Walker cases, helped end slavery in Massachusetts; Chief Justice Cushing, 1783.
Paid worker for the Sedgwicks; midwife, healer and nurse; bought her own house.
Died 28 Dec 1829; buried in the Sedgwick family plot in Stockbridge, the only non-family member.
